rationale: A wins because it does the boring adult work: it keeps the story inside the facts and tells the founder exactly what proof will survive a reporter call. A's best line is the proof demand under “Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions” asking whether savings were “realized versus merely flagged”; B's weakest habit shows up in “the auto-renewal, long the SaaS vendor's quiet profit center,” which is a nice sentence sitting on a fact the update did not give it. B has bones, but A has guardrails.
gaps_in_A: “Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions” overstates the product. The update says the agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves, not that it cancels subscriptions itself.

“charging for the approval workflow” is directionally plausible but still an inference. The update says an enterprise tier with custom approval workflows is coming later this year; it does not give pricing or confirm the exact monetization boundary.
The set leans hard on the launch as the why-now. It admits “No current news signal was supplied,” which is honest, but it means these are strong launch angles, not yet strong newsjack angles.
gaps_in_B: “long the SaaS vendor's quiet profit center” is invented color. The update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals; it does not prove auto-renewals are a profit center.
“a meaningful share of SaaS revenue is renewal inertia” is a reporter-killing overclaim. No revenue-share data was supplied.
“the enterprise tier is the real business” and “land-and-expand move” outrun the facts. Useful hypothesis, bad headline unless Ramp gives pricing and strategy on record.
“bot reading the fine print” implies contract parsing that the update never states. The agent scans spend and drafts emails; don't add product capabilities because the sentence sounds better.
